quiz.prompt: Your Node API becomes unresponsive while one request hashes a password with a synchronous function. Why?
choices: Node starts a thread per request
The synchronous work occupies the single JavaScript thread, so no other callback can run
quiz.explanation: Use the async variant (which runs in the libuv thread pool) or a worker thread for CPU-heavy work.

flashcards.front: Task versus microtask
flashcards.back: Tasks are timers, I/O callbacks and immediates; microtasks are promise reactions and queueMicrotask. All pending microtasks run after each task.

flashcards.front: Order of sync code, nextTick, promise callback and setTimeout 0 in a Node CommonJS script
flashcards.back: Synchronous code, then the nextTick queue, then promise callbacks, then the timer.

flashcards.front: Which part of a promise runs synchronously?
flashcards.back: The executor passed to the constructor. Every then, catch and finally callback is asynchronous.

flashcards.front: Three ways a then callback can settle the promise it returns
flashcards.back: Returning a value fulfils it, returning a promise makes it follow that promise, and throwing rejects it.

flashcards.front: What does await actually suspend?
flashcards.back: Only its own async function. The thread returns to the event loop and other work continues until the promise settles.

flashcards.front: Why does CPU-heavy synchronous code hurt a Node server?
flashcards.back: Every request shares one JavaScript thread, so nothing else is served until the heavy function returns.

flashcards.front: What is microtask starvation?
flashcards.back: Microtasks that keep scheduling more microtasks never let the loop reach timers or I/O. Yield through a real task instead.

flashcards.front: setTimeout 0 versus setImmediate
flashcards.back: Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs first; in the main module their order is not guaranteed.

topics.title: async/await patterns
topics.summary: Sequential versus parallel awaits, Promise.all, allSettled, race and any, the async forEach trap, bounded concurrency, retries with backoff and cancellation with AbortController.
topics.lesson:
## Sequential versus parallel

```js
// sequential: ~200 ms (each await waits for the previous one)
const user = await getUser(id);
const prefs = await getPrefs(id);

// parallel: ~100 ms (both start before either is awaited)
const [user, prefs] = await Promise.all([getUser(id), getPrefs(id)]);
```

Await in sequence only when a call needs the previous result. Independent calls should start together.

## The four combinators

- `Promise.all(ps)`: fulfils with an array of values in INPUT order; rejects as soon as ANY rejects (fail-fast; the other operations keep running, their results are ignored).
- `Promise.allSettled(ps)`: always fulfils, with `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` / `{ status: 'rejected', reason }` per input. Use it for "send all notifications, report which failed".
- `Promise.race(ps)`: settles like the FIRST promise to settle, fulfilled or rejected (timeouts, topic 12).
- `Promise.any(ps)`: fulfils with the first FULFILMENT; rejects with an `AggregateError` (with `.errors`) only if all reject. Use it for "try three mirrors, take the first that works".

## The async forEach trap

```js
items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); });
console.log('done');   // runs BEFORE any save finished; errors become unhandled rejections
```

`forEach` ignores the promises its callback returns. Use `for (const item of items) await save(item)` for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map(save))` for parallel.

## Bounded concurrency

`Promise.all(10000 ids.map(fetch))` opens 10,000 connections at once and gets you rate-limited. Limit how many run at a time: keep N "workers" that each pull the next item until the list is empty. Libraries like p-limit do this; it is a common interview exercise.

## Retries with backoff

Retry only **transient** failures (timeouts, 503, connection resets), never validation errors. Wait longer each time (exponential backoff: 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms), add random **jitter** so clients do not retry in lockstep, and cap the number of attempts. Retried writes must be **idempotent** (an idempotency key on POST /payments).

## Cancellation with AbortController

```js
const ac = new AbortController();
const res = await fetch(url, { signal: ac.signal });   // ac.abort() rejects with an AbortError
await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) }); // built-in timeout signal
```

Pass a signal down through your own async functions and check `signal.aborted` (or listen for `'abort'`) so work stops when a client disconnects or a user navigates away.

## Error handling

`try/catch` around `await` catches rejections. With `Promise.all`, one try/catch catches the first failure; use `allSettled` when you need every outcome. Never leave a promise un-awaited unless you attach a `.catch`.

quiz.prompt: Two independent 100 ms calls: `const a = await f(); const b = await g();` takes about how long?
quiz.explanation: The second call does not start until the first finished. Start both and await Promise.all to take about 100 ms.

quiz.prompt: What does `Promise.all([ok(1), fail("boom"), slowOk(3)])` do?
choices: Rejects with "boom" as soon as it rejects
quiz.explanation: Promise.all is fail-fast. The other operations still run; their results are just ignored.

quiz.prompt: Which combinator ALWAYS fulfils and reports each outcome?
quiz.explanation: allSettled gives { status, value } or { status, reason } for every input.

quiz.prompt: What does `Promise.any` reject with when every input rejects?
choices: An AggregateError holding all the errors
quiz.explanation: any only rejects when nothing fulfilled, and then reports every reason in .errors.

quiz.prompt: `items.forEach(async (i) => { await save(i); }); console.log("done");` When does "done" print?
choices: Before the saves finish: forEach does not wait for async callbacks
quiz.explanation: forEach ignores returned promises. Use for...of with await, or Promise.all over map.

quiz.prompt: Which failures should an automatic retry handle?
choices: Transient ones like timeouts, 503s and connection resets
quiz.explanation: Retrying a request that will deterministically fail again only adds load. Retry transient failures, with backoff and a cap.

quiz.prompt: Why add random jitter to retry delays?
choices: So many clients that failed together do not all retry at the same instant
quiz.explanation: Synchronised retries create thundering herds that knock the recovering service down again.

quiz.prompt: What makes a retried POST /payments safe?
choices: An idempotency key the server uses to deduplicate the request
quiz.explanation: Without idempotency a retry after a lost response can charge the customer twice.

quiz.prompt: Which API cancels an in-flight fetch?
choices: An AbortController signal passed in the fetch options, then controller.abort()
quiz.explanation: Promises themselves cannot be cancelled; AbortSignal is the standard cancellation channel.

quiz.prompt: Fetching 10,000 URLs with `Promise.all(urls.map(fetch))` is risky because...
choices: Results come back out of order
Every request starts at once: you exhaust sockets and hit rate limits
quiz.explanation: Bound the concurrency: a small pool of workers pulling from the list keeps throughput high without flooding the server.

flashcards.front: When should awaits run in sequence?
flashcards.back: Only when a call needs the previous call's result. Independent work should start together and be awaited with Promise.all.

flashcards.front: Promise.all versus Promise.allSettled
flashcards.back: all fails fast on the first rejection and gives values in input order; allSettled waits for everything and reports every fulfilment and rejection.

flashcards.front: Promise.race versus Promise.any
flashcards.back: race settles like whichever input settles first, even a rejection; any waits for the first fulfilment and only fails if all fail.

flashcards.front: Why is an async callback in forEach a bug?
flashcards.back: forEach discards the returned promises, so nothing waits for them and their errors go unhandled.

flashcards.front: How does bounded concurrency work?
flashcards.back: Start a fixed number of workers; each repeatedly takes the next unprocessed item until none remain, writing results back by index.

flashcards.front: The ingredients of a good retry policy
flashcards.back: Retry only transient failures, wait exponentially longer with jitter, cap the attempts, and make the operation idempotent.

flashcards.front: How do you cancel async work in JavaScript?
flashcards.back: Pass an AbortSignal down the call chain; abort() rejects signal-aware APIs like fetch, and your code checks signal.aborted.

flashcards.front: What does AbortSignal.timeout give you?
flashcards.back: A signal that aborts itself after the given milliseconds, a one-line timeout for fetch and other signal-aware APIs.

topics.title: Iterators & generators
topics.summary: The iteration protocol behind for...of and spread, single-use iterators, generator functions that produce values lazily, early exit and cleanup, and async generators for paged data.

quiz.prompt: What does `for (const x of { a: 1 }) {}` do?
choices: Throws TypeError: object is not iterable
quiz.explanation: Plain objects do not implement Symbol.iterator. Iterate Object.keys, values or entries instead.

quiz.prompt: `function* g() { console.log("start"); yield 1; }` What does `const it = g();` print?
choices: Nothing: the body runs only when next() is called
quiz.explanation: Calling a generator function only creates the generator object; its body is lazy.

quiz.prompt: `function* pair() { yield 1; yield 2; } const it = pair();` What are `[...it]` and then `[...it]` again?
quiz.explanation: An iterator is single-use: the first spread exhausts it.

quiz.prompt: `function* g() { yield 1; return 99; }` What is `[...g()]`?
quiz.explanation: The return value arrives with done: true, and spread and for...of ignore done results.

quiz.prompt: A generator has `try { yield 1; yield 2; } finally { cleanup(); }`. A for...of loop over it breaks after the first value. Does cleanup run?
choices: Yes: breaking calls the iterator's return(), which runs finally
quiz.explanation: for...of closes the iterator on break, return or throw, so generator finally blocks run.

quiz.prompt: What does `it.next()` return after a generator has finished?
quiz.explanation: A finished iterator keeps answering done: true.

quiz.prompt: Why can `function* naturals() { let n = 0; while (true) yield n++; }` be used safely?
choices: It produces values only as the consumer asks for them
It runs in a worker thread
quiz.explanation: Generators are lazy, so an infinite sequence is fine as long as the consumer stops pulling.

quiz.prompt: Which syntax consumes an async generator?
quiz.explanation: Async iterables need for await...of; spread and for...of only work with synchronous iterables.

quiz.prompt: What does `yield* other` do inside a generator?
choices: Yields the other iterable as a single value
Throws if other is an array
Yields each value of the other iterable in turn
quiz.explanation: yield* delegates: it forwards every value of the inner iterable (or generator).

quiz.prompt: Which method makes an object usable in for...of?
quiz.explanation: The iterable protocol is a Symbol.iterator method that returns an object with next().

flashcards.front: Iterable versus iterator
flashcards.back: An iterable has a Symbol.iterator method that hands out iterators; an iterator has next() returning value and done, and is used up once consumed.

flashcards.front: Which built-ins are iterable?
flashcards.back: Arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, typed arrays, arguments and generator objects. Plain objects are not.

flashcards.front: When does a generator's body run?
flashcards.back: Piece by piece: each next() call runs it up to the following yield. Creating the generator runs none of it.

flashcards.front: What happens to a generator's return value in for...of?
flashcards.back: It is ignored: it comes with done set to true, which ends the loop without being delivered.

flashcards.front: How does early exit from for...of clean up?
flashcards.back: The loop calls the iterator's return method, so any finally block inside the generator still runs.

flashcards.front: Why use generators for data pipelines?
flashcards.back: They process one item at a time on demand, so huge or endless sources never need to fit in memory.

flashcards.front: What are async generators good for?
flashcards.back: Producing values that need awaiting between them, such as the items of a paginated API, consumed with for await.

flashcards.front: What does yield* delegate to?
flashcards.back: Any iterable: it re-yields every value of the inner iterable or generator before continuing.

topics.title: TypeScript: types & narrowing
topics.summary: Structural typing, excess property checks, unknown versus any, unions and narrowing with typeof, in, instanceof and discriminants, exhaustive checks with never, and why types vanish at runtime.
topics.lesson:
## Types are structural and erased

TypeScript checks **shapes**: any value with the required properties fits a type, whatever it was declared as. And every type is **erased** at compile time: at runtime there is only JavaScript. You cannot ask "is this a User?" with a type; you must check the data.

```ts
interface User { id: string; name: string; email?: string }

const extra = { id: '1', name: 'a', role: 'admin' };
const ok: User = extra;                                     // fine: it has id and name
const bad: User = { id: '1', name: 'a', role: 'admin' };    // error: excess property 'role'
```

The **excess property check** applies only to a fresh object literal assigned directly: it catches typos like `emial`.

## Optional properties and strict null checks

`email?: string` has type `string | undefined`. With `strict` on (always turn it on), you must handle undefined before using it: `user.email ?? 'none'` or an `if`.

## any versus unknown

- `any` switches checking off: `an.toUpperCase()` compiles even if `an` is a number. It spreads silently.
- `unknown` means "could be anything, prove it first": `un.toUpperCase()` is an error until you narrow. Use `unknown` for `JSON.parse` results, `catch` variables and external input.

## Unions and narrowing

A value of type `string | number` only allows what both members allow. **Narrowing** refines the type inside a branch:

```ts
function format(v: string | number) {
  if (typeof v === 'string') return v.toUpperCase();   // v: string here
  return v.toFixed(2);                                  // v: number here
}
```

Narrowing tools: `typeof`, `instanceof`, `'key' in obj`, equality checks, truthiness, and **user-defined type guards**: `function isUser(x: unknown): x is User`.

## Discriminated unions

Give each variant a literal **tag**, and switching on it narrows to that variant:

```ts
type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; r: number } | { kind: 'square'; side: number };

function area(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case 'circle': return Math.PI * s.r ** 2;
    case 'square': return s.side ** 2;
    default: { const never: never = s; return never; }   // exhaustive check
  }
}
```

Add a `{ kind: 'tri' }` variant later and the `never` assignment becomes a compile error at every switch that forgot it. That is how unions model API results (`{ ok: true; data } | { ok: false; error }`), events and reducer actions safely.

## Literal types and as const

`const method = 'GET'` has the literal type `'GET'`; `let method = 'GET'` widens to `string`. `as const` makes arrays and objects deeply readonly with literal types: `['a', 'b'] as const` is `readonly ['a', 'b']`.

## Assertions do not check anything

`value as User` tells the compiler "trust me"; it converts and validates nothing. `'hello' as unknown as number` compiles. Data from HTTP requests, the database or `JSON.parse` must be **validated at runtime** (hand-written guards, or a schema library such as Zod that produces both the check and the type). This is the single most common TypeScript bug in CRUD code: typing a request body is not validating it.

## interface versus type

Both describe object shapes. Interfaces can be **merged** (two `interface X` declarations combine) and extended; `type` aliases cannot be redeclared but can express unions, tuples and mapped types. Pick one convention per codebase.

quiz.prompt: `const u: User = { id: "1", name: "a", role: "admin" };` (User has id and name) gives...
choices: An error only if role is undefined
quiz.explanation: Fresh object literals assigned directly get an excess property check, which catches typos.

quiz.prompt: Assigning a VARIABLE `extra` holding `{ id, name, role }` to a `User`...
choices: Compiles: TypeScript is structural and the excess check applies only to fresh literals
quiz.explanation: A value with at least the required properties is assignable; extra properties are allowed when not a fresh literal.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about `unknown` versus `any` is true?
choices: unknown must be narrowed before use; any disables checking
any must be narrowed; unknown is unchecked
quiz.explanation: unknown forces you to prove what a value is; any silently turns the type checker off.

quiz.prompt: Inside `if (typeof v === "string") { ... }` where `v: string | number`, the type of v is...
quiz.explanation: typeof checks narrow the union inside the branch (and to number in the other branch).

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of `const never: never = s;` in the default branch of a switch over a discriminated union?
choices: Compile-time exhaustiveness: it errors when a variant is not handled
quiz.explanation: If every variant is handled, s is never there; a new unhandled variant makes the assignment a type error.

quiz.prompt: What does `const user = req.body as User;` guarantee at runtime?
choices: That body has every User field
Nothing: assertions are erased and validate nothing
That body was parsed as JSON
quiz.explanation: Types vanish at runtime. Validate external input with a guard or a schema library.

quiz.prompt: With `strict`, what is the type of `user.email` when `email?: string`?
quiz.explanation: Optional properties may be missing, so TypeScript adds undefined to their type.

quiz.prompt: `const method = "GET"` versus `let method = "GET"`: what are their types?
quiz.explanation: const keeps the literal type because it cannot change; let widens to string.

quiz.prompt: What does `function isUser(x: unknown): x is User` add over returning boolean?
choices: Callers get x narrowed to User inside an if (isUser(x)) block
quiz.explanation: A type predicate tells the compiler what a true result proves. You still write the actual checks.

quiz.prompt: Which can be declared twice and merge into one?
quiz.explanation: Interfaces merge (declaration merging); redeclaring a type alias is a duplicate identifier error.

flashcards.front: What does structural typing mean?
flashcards.back: Compatibility is decided by shape: any value with the required members fits, regardless of how it was declared or constructed.

flashcards.front: When does the excess property check fire?
flashcards.back: Only for a fresh object literal assigned straight to a typed target; it exists to catch misspelled properties.

flashcards.front: Why prefer unknown over any for external data?
flashcards.back: unknown forces a check before use, while any silently disables type checking wherever the value flows.

flashcards.front: Five ways to narrow a union
flashcards.back: typeof, instanceof, an in check, comparing a discriminant tag, and a user-defined type guard function.

flashcards.front: What is a discriminated union?
flashcards.back: A union whose variants share a literal tag property, so checking the tag narrows to exactly one variant.

flashcards.front: How do you get exhaustiveness checking?
flashcards.back: In the fallback branch, assign the narrowed value to a variable of type never; any unhandled variant becomes a compile error.

flashcards.front: Do TypeScript types validate request bodies?
flashcards.back: No. They are erased before running; validate at runtime with guards or a schema library and derive the type from the schema.

flashcards.front: What does as const do?
flashcards.back: It freezes inference: literal types instead of string or number, and readonly arrays, tuples and properties.

topics.title: TypeScript: generics & utility types
topics.summary: Generic functions and constraints, keyof and indexed access types, the utility types you use daily (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Readonly, ReturnType, Awaited), and deriving types instead of repeating them.
topics.lesson:
## Generics: types as parameters

```ts
function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined { return xs[0]; }
first([1, 2])        // T inferred as number: returns number | undefined
first(['a'])         // string | undefined
```

A generic keeps the relationship between input and output. Without it you would write `any[] => any` and lose every check downstream.

**Constraints** say what a type parameter must have:

```ts
function byId<T extends { id: string }>(xs: T[], id: string): T | undefined {
  return xs.find((x) => x.id === id);   // x.id is allowed because of the constraint
}
byId([{ id: 1 }], '1');   // error: number is not assignable to string
```

## keyof and indexed access

```ts
type Keys = keyof { a: 1; b: 2 };           // 'a' | 'b'
function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] { return obj[key]; }
get({ id: 1, name: 'x' }, 'name')            // string
get({ id: 1, name: 'x' }, 'nope')            // error
```

`T[K]` (indexed access) is "the type of property K of T".

## The utility types

```ts
interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; passwordHash: string }

Partial<User>                  // every property optional: PATCH bodies
Required<T>                    // every property required
Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>      // only those keys
Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>     // everything except: public DTOs
Record<'draft' | 'live', number>  // an object with exactly those keys
Readonly<User>                 // assignments to properties are errors
ReturnType<typeof makeUser>    // the return type of a function
Awaited<Promise<Promise<string>>> // string: unwraps promises, recursively
NonNullable<string | null | undefined> // string
```

These are all compile-time only. `Readonly` does not freeze anything at runtime, and `Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>` does not remove the field from an object you send: you still have to build the DTO without it (`const { passwordHash, ...publicUser } = user`).

## Derive types instead of repeating them

Keep one source of truth and derive the rest:

```ts
const ROLES = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const;
type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number];            // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'

type CreateUser = Omit<User, 'id'>;            // POST body
type UpdateUser = Partial<CreateUser>;         // PATCH body
type UserRow = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof db.users.findFirst>>;
```

Change `User` once and every derived type follows.

## Mapped and conditional types (reading level)

`Partial` is itself a mapped type: `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`. Conditional types branch on types: `T extends string ? 'text' : 'other'`. You will read them in library typings more than you write them.

## Where generics show up in CRUD code

A typed API client `get<T>(url): Promise<T>` (remember: the T is a promise, not a validation), repository interfaces `Repo<T extends { id: string }>`, React components `<Select<T> items={T[]} />`, and `Result<T, E>` unions for error handling.

quiz.prompt: What is the return type of `first([1, 2])` for `function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined`?
quiz.explanation: T is inferred from the argument as number, and the signature keeps the relationship.

quiz.prompt: Why does `byId([{ id: 1 }], "1")` fail for `byId<T extends { id: string }>`?
choices: The element's id is a number, which violates the constraint
quiz.explanation: The constraint requires every T to have a string id.

quiz.prompt: What is `keyof { a: 1; b: 2 }`?
quiz.explanation: keyof gives the union of an object type's property names.

quiz.prompt: Which utility type best describes a PATCH body where any field may be sent?
quiz.explanation: Partial makes every property optional.

quiz.prompt: A `Record<"a" | "b", number>` is assigned `{ a: 1 }`. Result?
quiz.explanation: Record with a union of keys requires every key in the union.

quiz.prompt: `res.json(user as Omit<User, "passwordHash">)` — is the hash removed from the response?
choices: No: types are erased; the object still contains the field
Only if the field is optional
quiz.explanation: Utility types change what the compiler believes, not the data. Destructure the field out or map to a DTO.

quiz.prompt: What is `Awaited<Promise<Promise<string>>>`?
quiz.explanation: Awaited unwraps promise types recursively, mirroring what await does at runtime.

quiz.prompt: `const ROLES = ["admin", "viewer"] as const; type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number];` What is Role?
quiz.explanation: as const keeps the literals, and indexing the tuple type with number gives the union of its elements.

quiz.prompt: Does `Readonly<User>` stop a property from being changed at runtime?
choices: Yes, but only in strict mode
No: it is a compile-time check only; use Object.freeze for runtime
quiz.explanation: Readonly makes assignments type errors; the generated JavaScript is unchanged.

quiz.prompt: In `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, what does `T[K]` mean?
choices: The type of property K of T
quiz.explanation: Indexed access types look up a property's type, so get returns exactly the type of the requested field.

flashcards.front: Why use a generic instead of any?
flashcards.back: A generic keeps the link between input and output types, so callers get precise types back; any discards checking everywhere it flows.

flashcards.front: What does a constraint like T extends { id: string } do?
flashcards.back: It limits which types may be used for T and lets the function body use the members the constraint guarantees.

flashcards.front: Partial, Required and Readonly
flashcards.back: Make every property optional, make every property mandatory, and forbid assignment to properties, all at compile time.

flashcards.front: Pick versus Omit
flashcards.back: Pick keeps only the named keys; Omit keeps all keys except the named ones.

flashcards.front: What does Record<K, V> describe?
flashcards.back: An object type with exactly the keys in K, each holding a V; with a union of literal keys, every key is required.

flashcards.front: ReturnType and Awaited together
flashcards.back: ReturnType reads a function's return type; wrapping it in Awaited unwraps the promise an async function returns.

flashcards.front: Do utility types change runtime objects?
flashcards.back: Never. An Omit type does not remove a field from the data; you still have to build the object without it.

flashcards.front: How do you turn a constant list into a union type?
flashcards.back: Declare the array with as const and index its type with number to get the union of its literal elements.

topics.title: Node core: fs, path, process, events & streams
topics.summary: The Node building blocks behind every backend: promise-based fs, path.join versus resolve, process.env strings, synchronous EventEmitter events and the error event, Buffers and bytes, and streams with backpressure.
topics.lesson:
## fs: use the promise API

```js
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
const text = await readFile(new URL('./config.json', import.meta.url), 'utf8');
```

The `*Sync` functions block the whole process (topic 12): fine in a CLI or at startup, wrong inside a request handler. Relative paths in fs calls resolve against `process.cwd()` (where the process was started), NOT the file's folder; build paths from `import.meta.dirname` (or `__dirname` in CommonJS).

## path

```js
path.join('a', '../b')        // 'b'         joins and normalises
path.join('/a/', '/b')        // '/a/b'
path.resolve('/x', 'y', '../z') // '/x/z'    builds an ABSOLUTE path, right to left
path.resolve('/x', '/y')      // '/y'        a later absolute segment restarts
path.extname('a.tar.gz')      // '.gz'
```

Never concatenate paths with `+ '/'`; and never join untrusted input into a path without checking the result stays inside your base folder (path traversal: `../../etc/passwd`).

## process

- `process.env` values are **always strings** (or undefined). `process.env.PORT = 3000` stores `'3000'`, and `'false'` is truthy. Parse and validate configuration once at startup.
- `process.argv`: `[nodePath, scriptPath, ...args]`.
- `process.exitCode = 1` lets the process finish its work and exit non-zero; `process.exit()` kills it immediately, possibly losing buffered output.
- Signals: listen for `SIGTERM` to shut down gracefully (stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close the DB pool).

## EventEmitter

```js
const e = new EventEmitter();
e.on('saved', (doc) => log(doc.id));
e.emit('saved', doc);   // listeners run SYNCHRONOUSLY, in registration order, before emit returns
```

- `emit` returns `true` if there were listeners.
- `once` removes the listener after its first call.
- Emitting `'error'` with **no** `'error'` listener throws the error, which usually crashes the process. Always attach error listeners to streams, sockets and emitters you create.
- Forgetting to remove listeners in long-lived objects leaks memory (Node warns after 10 listeners for one event).

## Buffer: bytes, not characters

`Buffer.byteLength('é')` is 2 while `'é'.length` is 1. HTTP `Content-Length`, file sizes and database column limits count **bytes** in UTF-8. Splitting a Buffer at an arbitrary byte can cut a multi-byte character in half; decode text with a streaming decoder or by lines.

## Streams and backpressure

Streams process data piece by piece: read a 5 GB file with constant memory. Readable streams are async iterables:

```js
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
await pipeline(createReadStream('in.csv'), transformRows, createWriteStream('out.csv'));
```

`pipeline` connects streams, forwards errors from any stage and destroys every stream on failure. **Backpressure**: when a writable stream's buffer is full, `write()` returns false and the producer should wait for `'drain'`; `pipeline` and `for await` handle this for you, a manual `on('data')` loop does not. Chunks are arbitrary slices: a line or a JSON record can span two chunks, so keep the incomplete tail between chunks.

quiz.prompt: What is `path.join("a", "../b")`?
quiz.explanation: join concatenates and normalises, resolving the .. segment.

quiz.prompt: What does `path.resolve("/x", "/y")` return?
quiz.explanation: resolve works right to left and stops at the first absolute segment it meets.

quiz.prompt: After `process.env.FEATURE = false`, what is `typeof process.env.FEATURE` and is it truthy?
quiz.explanation: Environment variables are always strings, and the non-empty string "false" is truthy. Parse config explicitly.

quiz.prompt: When do EventEmitter listeners run?
choices: Synchronously, inside emit(), in registration order
quiz.explanation: emit calls each listener directly before returning; use setImmediate inside a listener if work must be deferred.

quiz.prompt: What happens on `emitter.emit("error", err)` when no "error" listener is registered?
choices: The error is thrown, typically crashing the process
It is logged as a warning
quiz.explanation: The error event is special: unhandled, it throws. Attach error listeners to every emitter and stream.

quiz.prompt: What are `Buffer.byteLength('é')` and `'é'.length`?
quiz.explanation: UTF-8 encodes é in two bytes, while length counts UTF-16 code units.

quiz.prompt: A relative path in `readFile("./data.json")` is resolved against...
choices: The current working directory of the process
quiz.explanation: Use import.meta.dirname (or __dirname) to build paths relative to the source file.

quiz.prompt: Why use `pipeline()` instead of chaining `.pipe()` calls?
choices: It forwards errors from every stage and destroys all the streams on failure
quiz.explanation: With .pipe() an error in the middle leaves other streams open and unhandled.

quiz.prompt: What is backpressure?
choices: The consumer signalling the producer to pause because its buffer is full
quiz.explanation: write() returns false when the buffer is full; producers should wait for drain. pipeline and for await handle it.

quiz.prompt: Why can a readable stream of text split a line in two?
choices: Chunks are arbitrary slices of the data, not aligned to lines or records
quiz.explanation: Keep the incomplete tail of each chunk and prepend it to the next one.

flashcards.front: path.join versus path.resolve
flashcards.back: join glues segments and normalises them; resolve builds an absolute path, starting over at the right-most absolute segment.

flashcards.front: What type are environment variables?
flashcards.back: Always strings or undefined. Numbers and booleans must be parsed, and the string false is still truthy.

flashcards.front: process.exit() versus process.exitCode
flashcards.back: exit stops immediately and can drop buffered output; setting exitCode lets pending work finish and then exits with that code.

flashcards.front: How does EventEmitter deliver events?
flashcards.back: Synchronously during emit, to every listener in the order they were added.

flashcards.front: Why attach an error listener to every stream and emitter?
flashcards.back: An error event with no listener is thrown, which normally brings down the whole process.

flashcards.front: Bytes versus characters in Node
flashcards.back: Content-Length, file sizes and many column limits count UTF-8 bytes; JavaScript string length counts UTF-16 code units.

flashcards.front: What does stream.pipeline give you?
flashcards.back: Streams wired together with backpressure, errors from any stage propagated, and every stream cleaned up on failure.

flashcards.front: Why avoid the Sync fs functions in request handlers?
flashcards.back: They block the single JavaScript thread, so every other request waits until the file operation finishes.

topics.title: HTTP APIs in Node
topics.summary: Methods and idempotency, the status codes that matter, routes and query strings, middleware order and error middleware, validating bodies at the boundary, and pagination.
topics.lesson:
## Methods and their promises

| method | use | safe | idempotent |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | read | yes | yes |
| POST | create / run an action | no | no |
| PUT | replace a resource at a known URL | no | yes |
| PATCH | partial update | no | not necessarily |
| DELETE | remove | no | yes |

**Idempotent** means repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once (DELETE twice: still deleted). Clients, proxies and retry logic rely on that; a non-idempotent POST needs an idempotency key to be retried safely.

## Status codes that matter

- **200** OK, **201** Created (send a `Location` header with the new resource URL), **204** No Content (successful DELETE or an update with no body).
- **400** Bad Request (malformed or invalid input), **401** Unauthorized (not authenticated: missing or bad credentials), **403** Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), **404** Not Found, **409** Conflict (duplicate key, stale version), **422** Unprocessable Content (well-formed but semantically invalid; some APIs use it instead of 400 for validation), **429** Too Many Requests (send `Retry-After`).
- **500** for unexpected server failures (never leak internals, topic 10), **503** when temporarily unavailable.

## URLs: routes, params and query strings

```js
const u = new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost');
u.pathname                     // '/users/42'
u.searchParams.get('page')     // '2'  <- a STRING (or null when absent)
new URLSearchParams('tag=a&tag=b').getAll('tag')  // ['a', 'b']
new URLSearchParams('q=x+y').get('q')             // 'x y': + decodes to a space
```

Route parameters (`/users/:id`) and query values are **strings**: convert and validate them (`?page=abc` must be a 400, not `NaN` reaching the database). Path segments are percent-encoded: `decodeURIComponent('caf%C3%A9')` is `'café'`, and malformed encodings throw a `URIError`, which is also a 400.

## Middleware

Frameworks like Express run middleware **in registration order**: each one handles the request or calls `next()`. Order matters: body parsing before handlers that read the body, authentication before authorisation, the 404 handler after every route, and the **error handler last**. In Express an error handler is recognised by its four parameters `(err, req, res, next)`; any `next(err)` (or, in Express 5, a rejected async handler) jumps straight to it.

## Validate at the boundary

Parse, validate and normalise once, at the edge: types of every field, required fields, string lengths, enum values, number ranges. Respond 400 (or 422) with field-level messages. **Allow-list** fields: never `Object.assign(user, req.body)`, which lets a client set `role: 'admin'` (mass assignment).

## Pagination

- **Offset**: `?limit=20&offset=40`. Simple, but slow for deep pages and unstable while rows are inserted.
- **Cursor**: `?limit=20&after=<opaque cursor>` based on a sort key (id or created_at plus id). Stable and fast for infinite scroll.

Always cap `limit` server-side and return a stable sort order.

## Response conventions

`Content-Type: application/json`, a consistent error body (problem details: `{ title, status, detail, errors }`), ISO-8601 timestamps in UTC, and ids as strings. Return 404 rather than 403 for resources the caller must not even know exist.

quiz.prompt: Which methods are idempotent?
quiz.explanation: Repeating GET, PUT or DELETE leaves the same state; POST creates again, and PATCH may not be idempotent.

quiz.prompt: A POST /orders succeeds. Which response is most correct?
choices: 201 Created with a Location header for the new order
quiz.explanation: 201 signals a created resource; Location tells the client its URL.

quiz.prompt: A logged-in user requests another tenant's invoice they may not see. What is the usual safest response?
choices: 403 or, to avoid revealing it exists, 404
quiz.explanation: 401 means not authenticated. For a resource the caller should not know exists, many APIs answer 404.

quiz.prompt: What does `new URLSearchParams('page=2').get('page')` return?
quiz.explanation: Query values are always strings (or null). Convert and validate before use.

quiz.prompt: What does `new URLSearchParams('q=x+y').get('q')` return?
quiz.explanation: In query strings '+' decodes to a space; a literal plus is sent as %2B.

quiz.prompt: In Express, how is an error-handling middleware recognised?
choices: By having four parameters: (err, req, res, next)
quiz.explanation: Express checks the function arity; register it after the routes.

quiz.prompt: Why is `Object.assign(user, req.body)` in an update handler dangerous?
choices: It lets clients set fields they should never control, like role or isAdmin
quiz.explanation: This is mass assignment. Copy only an explicit allow-list of fields.

quiz.prompt: A client sends `?limit=100000`. What should the server do?
choices: Cap the limit at a server-side maximum (or reject it)
quiz.explanation: Unbounded page sizes let one request overload the database.

quiz.prompt: What does `decodeURIComponent("%E0%A4%A")` do?
choices: Throws a URIError, which a router should turn into a 400

flashcards.back: Sending the same request many times has the same effect on the server as sending it once.

flashcards.front: 401 versus 403
flashcards.back: 401: the caller is not authenticated (missing or invalid credentials). 403: authenticated, but not permitted to do this.

flashcards.front: When do you return 409?
flashcards.back: When a request conflicts with current state: a duplicate unique value, or an update based on a stale version.

flashcards.front: What type are route params and query values?
flashcards.back: Strings, or null when a query key is absent. Convert and validate them before they reach business logic.

flashcards.front: Why does middleware order matter?
flashcards.back: Each middleware sees only what earlier ones prepared, so parsing comes before handlers, auth before routes, and the error handler last.

flashcards.front: What is mass assignment and how do you prevent it?
flashcards.back: Copying a whole request body onto a model so clients can set privileged fields. Copy only an explicit list of allowed fields.

flashcards.front: Offset versus cursor pagination
flashcards.back: Offset is simple but slow deep down and shifts when rows are inserted; a cursor over a stable sort key is fast and consistent.

flashcards.front: What should a 201 response include?
flashcards.back: A Location header pointing at the new resource, usually with the created representation in the body.

topics.title: React: components, state & hooks
topics.summary: Components as functions of props and state, why state must be replaced rather than mutated, batching and functional updates, keys in lists, lifting state up, derived values, and the rules of hooks.
topics.lesson:
## Components are functions

A React component is a function that takes **props** and returns a description of the UI. React calls it whenever it needs to re-render: when the component's state changes, or its parent re-renders it. Rendering must be **pure**: same props and state, same output, no side effects in the body.

```jsx
function Counter({ step = 1 }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount((c) => c + step)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

Props are read-only inputs. A child never changes its props; it asks the parent to, through a callback prop.

## State: replace, never mutate

`useState` gives the current value and a setter. React decides whether to re-render by comparing the new value with the old one using `Object.is`:

```jsx
items.push(newItem); setItems(items);         // same array reference: React may skip the render
setItems([...items, newItem]);                // new array: re-render
setUser({ ...user, name: 'Ana' });            // new object with one field changed
```

Setting a state to an `Object.is`-equal value bails out of the update. Mutating state in place produces stale UI and bugs that are hard to trace.

## Updates are batched; use functional updates

Inside an event handler, React 18 batches every setter call and re-renders once afterwards. A setter does not change the variable in the current render:

```jsx
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);    // both read the same count: +1 in total
setCount((c) => c + 1);
setCount((c) => c + 1); // updater functions chain: +2
```

Use the updater form whenever the next state depends on the previous one.

## Lists need stable keys

`{orders.map((o) => <OrderRow key={o.id} order={o} />)}`. Keys tell React which item is which between renders. Using the array **index** as key breaks when items are inserted, removed or reordered: state (an input's text, a checkbox) sticks to the wrong row. Keys must be stable and unique among siblings.

## Lifting state up and derived values

When two components need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent and pass it down with callbacks. Do not copy props into state, and do not store what you can compute: a filtered list, a total, `isValid`. Compute it during render (wrap it in `useMemo` only if it is measurably expensive).

## Controlled inputs

`<input value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />`: the state is the single source of truth, and every keystroke flows through it, which makes validation and formatting straightforward.

## The rules of hooks

1. Call hooks only at the **top level** of a component or custom hook: never inside conditions, loops or after an early return. React identifies each hook by its call order.
2. Call hooks only from React functions (components and custom hooks named `useSomething`).

## useReducer for complex state

When updates involve several fields or many kinds of events (a cart, a multi-step form), `useReducer(reducer, initial)` centralises the logic in a **pure** function `(state, action) => newState`, which is easy to test without rendering anything.

quiz.prompt: Inside one click handler: `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);` with count 0. What is count after the re-render?
quiz.explanation: Both calls read the same count from this render. Use setCount((c) => c + 1) twice to add 2.

quiz.prompt: Why might `items.push(x); setItems(items);` fail to update the UI?
choices: push is not allowed in React
The array reference is unchanged, so React sees the same value and can skip the update
quiz.explanation: React compares with Object.is; create a new array: setItems([...items, x]).

quiz.prompt: Why is the array index a poor `key` for a list where rows can be removed?
choices: After a removal, indexes shift, so React reuses state of the wrong row
quiz.explanation: Keys identify items across renders; use a stable id from the data.

quiz.prompt: Which follows the rules of hooks?
choices: Calling useEffect inside a for loop
Calling useState after an early return
Calling every hook unconditionally at the top level of the component
quiz.explanation: React matches hooks by call order, so the order must be identical on every render.

quiz.prompt: Two sibling components both need the selected customer. Where should that state live?
choices: In both, kept in sync with effects
In their closest common parent, passed down as props
quiz.explanation: Lifting state up keeps one source of truth.

quiz.prompt: A component shows `orders.filter((o) => o.status === tab)`. Should the filtered list be stored in state?
choices: No: derive it during render from the existing state
Only if it has more than ten items
quiz.explanation: Storing derived data means keeping two copies in sync; compute it (memoise only if expensive).

quiz.prompt: What does React do when you call a state setter with a value `Object.is`-equal to the current state?
choices: Bails out: no re-render is needed
quiz.explanation: Equal state means nothing changed, so React can skip rendering that component.

quiz.prompt: What must a component body NOT do while rendering?
choices: Perform side effects like fetching data or changing external variables
quiz.explanation: Rendering must be pure; side effects belong in event handlers or effects.

quiz.prompt: What makes an input "controlled"?
choices: Its value comes from state and onChange updates that state
quiz.explanation: The state is the single source of truth for what the input shows.

quiz.prompt: Why is a reducer for useReducer written as a pure function?
choices: So the next state depends only on the current state and the action, which is predictable and easy to test
quiz.explanation: Pure reducers can be tested in isolation and replayed; mutation inside them causes the same stale-UI bugs as mutating state.

flashcards.front: How does React decide a state update changed something?
flashcards.back: It compares the new value with the old one using Object.is, so a mutated object or array looks unchanged.

flashcards.front: Why use the updater form of a state setter?
flashcards.back: Updater functions receive the latest pending state, so several updates in one handler chain correctly instead of overwriting each other.

flashcards.front: What are list keys for?
flashcards.back: They let React match items between renders. Keys must be stable and unique among siblings, typically a database id.

flashcards.front: What does lifting state up mean?
flashcards.back: Moving shared state to the nearest common parent and passing it, plus callbacks to change it, down as props.

flashcards.front: Why not store derived values in state?
flashcards.back: They can drift from their source. Recompute them during render, memoising only when the computation is expensive.

flashcards.front: The two rules of hooks
flashcards.back: Call hooks unconditionally at the top level, and only from components or custom hooks.

flashcards.front: When reach for useReducer over useState?
flashcards.back: When state has several related fields or many kinds of updates, so one pure reducer function owns all transitions.

flashcards.front: What does purity mean for a component?
flashcards.back: For the same props and state it returns the same output and has no side effects while rendering.

topics.title: React: effects, rendering & data fetching
topics.summary: When effects run, dependency arrays compared with Object.is, cleanup order, StrictMode double runs, stale closures, race conditions in fetch effects, and the effects you should not write at all.
topics.lesson:
## When effects run

`useEffect(fn, deps)` runs `fn` **after** React has committed the render to the screen, never during rendering. Then:

- no dependency array: after EVERY render
- `[]`: after the first render only (and its cleanup on unmount)
- `[a, b]`: after the first render, and after any render where `a` or `b` changed, compared with `Object.is`

If `fn` returns a function, that is the **cleanup**. React runs the previous cleanup **before** running the effect again, and on unmount. Subscriptions, timers, sockets and fetches all need cleanup.

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);
```

In development, **StrictMode** mounts, unmounts and re-mounts every component once, so each effect runs, cleans up, and runs again. An effect that breaks when run twice was already broken (it would leak or double-subscribe on fast navigation).

## Dependencies: Object.is all the way down

Objects, arrays and functions created during render are NEW every render, so an effect depending on them re-runs every time, and an effect that sets state from them can loop forever:

```jsx
const options = { userId };                  // new object each render
useEffect(() => { load(options); }, [options]);   // runs after every render
useEffect(() => { load({ userId }); }, [userId]);  // depend on the primitive instead
```

`useMemo` and `useCallback` keep a value or function identity stable between renders when it must be a dependency. `NaN` as a dependency is stable (`Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true); `0` and `-0` count as different.

## Stale closures

An effect or callback sees the props and state of the render that created it. An interval created once with `[]` that reads `count` keeps reading the FIRST render's `count` forever. Fixes: include the value in the dependencies, use the updater form `setCount((c) => c + 1)`, or keep a mutable `useRef`.

## Fetching in an effect: the race condition

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const ac = new AbortController();
  fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, { signal: ac.signal })
    .then((r) => r.json())
    .then(setUser)
    .catch((e) => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setError(e); });
  return () => ac.abort();   // id changed or unmounted: ignore the stale response
}, [id]);
```

Without cleanup, a slow response for an OLD id can arrive after the new one and overwrite it. In real apps a data-fetching library (TanStack Query, SWR) or the framework's loaders handle caching, deduping and races for you.

## You might not need an effect

- **Derived values**: compute during render (topic 19), not `useEffect(() => setFull(first + last), [first, last])`.
- **Responding to an event**: put the logic in the event handler, not in an effect watching a "submitted" flag.
- **Resetting state when an id changes**: give the component `key={id}` so React remounts it with fresh state.

Effects are for synchronising with things OUTSIDE React: the network, timers, the DOM, browser APIs, third-party widgets.

## Rendering, briefly

A state change re-renders that component and, by default, all of its children. Re-rendering is usually cheap; only optimise (`React.memo`, `useMemo`, moving state down, splitting components) when the profiler shows a real cost. Never mutate during render, and keep keys stable so React can preserve the right state.

quiz.prompt: When does an effect with dependency array `[]` run?
choices: After the first render only, with its cleanup on unmount
quiz.explanation: An empty array means no dependency can change, so the effect runs once after mounting.

quiz.prompt: When does an effect with NO dependency array run?
quiz.explanation: Without a dependency array React has nothing to compare, so it re-runs after every render.

quiz.prompt: In what order do the cleanup and the next run of an effect happen when its dependencies change?
choices: The new effect runs, then the old cleanup
The old cleanup runs first, then the new effect
quiz.explanation: React cleans up the previous effect before running it again with new values.

quiz.prompt: `const opts = { id }; useEffect(() => load(opts), [opts]);` What happens?
choices: The effect runs only when id changes
The effect runs after every render, because opts is a new object each time
quiz.explanation: Dependencies are compared with Object.is; depend on id (a primitive) or memoise opts.

quiz.prompt: Why does an effect run twice on mount in development?
choices: StrictMode mounts, unmounts and remounts to expose missing cleanup
quiz.explanation: StrictMode deliberately double-invokes effects in development; correct effects with cleanup behave the same.

quiz.prompt: A user switches from user 1 to user 2 quickly, and user 1's slow response arrives last. Without cleanup, what is shown?
quiz.explanation: The stale response wins the race. Abort the fetch or ignore its result in the cleanup.

quiz.prompt: An interval set up with `[]` deps logs `count` every second while count changes. What does it log?
choices: The count from the first render, forever (a stale closure)
quiz.explanation: The callback closed over the first render's count. Use the updater form, a ref, or proper dependencies.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT a good use of useEffect?
choices: Syncing with a third-party chart library
Computing fullName from firstName and lastName
quiz.explanation: Derived values should be computed during render; an effect adds an extra render and a window of inconsistent UI.

quiz.prompt: How do you reset a form component's state when the edited record id changes?
choices: Render it with key={id} so React remounts it
An effect that resets every field
Store the id in a ref
quiz.explanation: A new key gives a fresh component instance with fresh initial state.

quiz.prompt: Is a dependency of `NaN` treated as changed on every render?
quiz.explanation: React compares dependencies with Object.is, which treats NaN as equal to itself.

flashcards.front: The three dependency-array cases of useEffect
flashcards.back: No array: it re-runs following each render. Empty array: once after mount. With values: after mount and whenever a value changed by Object.is.

flashcards.front: When does an effect cleanup run?
flashcards.back: Before the effect runs again with new dependencies, and when the component unmounts.

flashcards.front: Why do objects and functions make troublesome dependencies?
flashcards.back: They are recreated on every render, so they always look changed. Depend on primitives or keep their identity with useMemo or useCallback.

flashcards.front: What is a stale closure in React?
flashcards.back: A callback or effect that keeps reading the props and state of the render that created it, because it was never recreated.

flashcards.front: How do you avoid race conditions when fetching in an effect?
flashcards.back: Abort the request or set an ignore flag in the cleanup, so a response for outdated inputs is never applied.

flashcards.front: Why does StrictMode run effects twice in development?
flashcards.back: To surface effects without proper cleanup; a correct effect behaves the same after a mount, unmount and remount.

flashcards.front: Three effects you usually do not need
flashcards.back: Computing derived data, reacting to user events (use the handler), and resetting state on a prop change (use a key).

flashcards.front: What are effects actually for?
flashcards.back: Synchronising a component with systems outside React: network, timers, subscriptions, the DOM and browser APIs.
